blockers: Requires legislation; the H-2A program has no statutory numerical cap and the H-2B cap is set by statute and adjusted by supplemental authority.
The Mandate itself records that some conservatives favor the programs, and agricultural and seasonal employers rely on them.

durability.why: The wage-rate and supplemental-visa actions are administrative and reversible; any cap would need a statute to be durable.

history.note: Read the FY2026 H-2B supplemental rule on the Federal Register (joint DHS and DOL, 64,716 visas, Public Law 119-37), resolving the earlier uncertainty, and added the 2026-08-03 H-2A wage rate update; no FY2027 supplemental or final H-2A wage rule found. Stage unchanged.

proposal: The Mandate recommends that Congress immediately cap the H-2A agricultural visa program at current levels and phase it down over 10 to 20 years (alongside an industry consortium to fund farm automation), and cap and phase out the H-2B seasonal nonagricultural program over no more than 10 years. It records alternative conservative views that favor keeping both programs.
remaining: Congress would need to enact a cap and a phase-down schedule for H-2A and H-2B; no such bill was searched for or found.
A farm-automation industry consortium with matching federal funds, as the Mandate recommends (no action found).

status_summary: No cap or phase-down was found. DOL issued an interim final rule on 2025-10-02 changing how H-2A wage rates are set (using BLS data in place of the discontinued USDA farm labor survey), citing labor shortage and food-supply concerns, and on 2026-08-03 published updated H-2A adverse effect wage rates under that methodology; the notice still describes the 2025 rule as interim, so no final rule was found. On 2026-02-03 DHS and DOL jointly published a temporary final rule (91 FR 5040) making up to 64,716 supplemental H-2B visas available for FY2026 on top of the 66,000 statutory limit, under authority extended by Public Law 119-37 (signed 2025-11-12) from Public Law 118-47; the visas are split into three allocations, mostly for returning workers early in the season, and are limited to employers attesting to permanent and severe financial loss. No supplemental rule for FY2027 was found in the Federal Register through 2026-10-13. Both actions keep or expand the programs, which runs opposite to the Mandate's recommendation to cap and reduce them; the Mandate also records alternative conservative views favoring the programs.

timeline.event: A federal court in Louisiana enters final judgment vacating DOL's 2023 H-2A wage-rate rule (Teche Vermilion Sugar Cane Growers v. Su), returning the program to the 2010 methodology, according to DOL's later rule.

DOL publishes an interim final rule, effective immediately, setting H-2A adverse effect wage rates for non-range occupations from BLS wage data by skill level instead of USDA survey data. DOL cites a claimed labor shortage tied to reduced illegal immigration and the end of the USDA survey; 887 comments were received by 2025-12-01. DOL reports H-2A worker requests rose from about 286,900 (FY2020) to about 391,600 (FY2024).

DHS and DOL jointly publish a temporary final rule (91 FR 5040, effective 2026-01-30 through 2026-09-30) making up to 64,716 supplemental H-2B visas available for FY2026 above the 66,000 statutory limit, under authority in Public Law 119-37 (signed 2025-11-12) extending Public Law 118-47; the visas come in three allocations, the first two for returning workers, and employers must attest to permanent and severe financial loss without the workers.

DOL's Employment and Training Administration publishes updated H-2A adverse effect wage rates for non-range occupations (91 FR 48946) under the methodology of the 2025-10-02 interim final rule, using BLS wage data released 2026-05-15 that represent May 2025 estimates (average rate 15.96 dollars), effective 2026-08-03, or 2026-08-17 for entities covered by the court order in Kansas et al. v. Department of Labor; the notice still describes the 2025 rule as interim.

title: Cap and phase down the H-2A and H-2B temporary worker visa programs
uncertainties: The FY2026 H-2B supplemental rule was read on 2026-10-13 (first 100,000 of about 106,000 characters): joint DHS and DOL temporary final rule, 91 FR 5040, up to 64,716 visas, authority from Public Law 119-37 extending Public Law 118-47; this resolves the earlier uncertainty about the visa number and issuing agencies. A Federal Register search for H-2B documents from 2026-02-04 to 2026-10-13 showed no FY2027 supplemental rule (only information collection notices), but FY2027 supplemental authority and any rule could still appear after that date or not be indexed under that term. The H-2A rule remains interim as of the 2026-08-03 notice; the court order in Kansas et al. v. Department of Labor, which the notice mentions for the effective date, was not examined. The effect of the H-2A wage change on wage levels was not verified and no characterization is made. A DOL proposed rule of 2026-03-27 on prevailing wages concerns H-1B, E-3 and PERM, not H-2A or H-2B (the visible text). Congressional bills to cap H-2A or H-2B were not searched. 'Diverged' reflects that the H-2B limit was raised, the opposite of the Mandate's cap; the H-2A action is a different design and not a direct reversal.
